match.reason: No existing point covers foreign direct and portfolio investment in Australia; the closest ones, e-investment on firms' investment decisions and e-bop on the current account, teach different ideas.

draft.title: Foreign investment in Australia
card: Foreign investment is money from overseas put into Australian assets. Australia has often spent more on investment than it has saved at home, so it draws on foreign funds to make up the gap.
a foreign investor buys a lasting stake in a business, such as a mine or a factory. It usually gives the investor a say in how the business is run.
a foreign investor buys shares or bonds, often to earn a return. It does not usually give the investor a say in running the business.
Both kinds bring in funds that Australian saving alone could not supply. They let projects go ahead that might not be built otherwise.
draft.remember: Direct investment is a lasting stake in a business. Portfolio investment is shares and bonds.

a.q: Which of these is an example of foreign direct investment in Australia?
opts: A Japanese company buys a coal mine in Queensland
A Swiss bank buys a few shares in an Australian bank
A fund in Canada buys Australian government bonds
A French saver buys shares in a Sydney retailer
a.why: Buying a mine gives the investor a lasting stake and a say in how it runs. The other three are purchases of shares or bonds, which are portfolio investment. A few shares in a bank do not give a say in running it.
a.clue: Which purchase gives the buyer a lasting stake in running a business?

b.q: Australian saving falls short of what a new gas project needs. A foreign company pays for the project and runs it. What kind of investment is this, and what does it show?
opts: Direct investment, funding what local saving cannot
Portfolio investment, funding what local saving cannot
Direct investment, replacing the need for any project
Portfolio investment, giving the investor a say in it
Direct investment, cutting what Australia must save
b.why: The company funds and runs the project, so it holds a lasting stake. That is direct investment. It fills the gap left by domestic saving. Portfolio investment is wrong because it means buying shares or bonds without usually having a say.
b.clue: Who runs the project, and where does the money come from?

a.best: A Japanese company buys a coal mine in Queensland

b.best: Direct investment, funding what local saving cannot

problems.detail: 'Portfolio investment is shares and bonds' suggests any share purchase is portfolio investment. Direct investment is often made by buying shares too: in Australian statistics, a holding of 10% or more of voting equity counts as direct. The card says the difference is a lasting stake and a say in running the business, not whether shares are bought.

The why says 'The other three are purchases of shares or bonds, which are portfolio investment', implying share purchases are always portfolio. It should say they are small holdings with no lasting stake or say in running the business, to match the card's distinction.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. However, the remember line and why (a) imply that buying shares is always portfolio investment, which is misleading, because direct investment often takes the form of a large shareholding.
